case.subject: Incident review
case.title: Payment API outage postmortem and actions

canvasName: R2-C07 Payment API outage postmortem and actions

segments.text: This is the postmortem for the payment API outage on Tuesday. The incident lasted fifty two minutes, from 14:07 to 14:59 UTC. During that window, about sixty percent of card payments failed, and some customers saw a generic error page. No money was lost, but we violated our error budget for the quarter and we need to understand both the technical cause and the process gaps. This meeting is blameless.
segments.textReply: I’m capturing the incident scope and impact first, with the blameless review principle explicit.

segments.text: We are here to find system problems, not to assign personal fault. Let's build the timeline. At 13:55, we deployed release 4.18.2, which included a small change to the connection pool settings. At 14:03, the first alert fired for elevated latency on the payment service. At 14:07, error rate crossed five percent. The on call engineer acknowledged at 14:09 and began checking dashboards.
segments.textReply: I’ll add the timeline as a separate panel below the overview, keeping the sequence factual and non-blaming.

segments.text: At 14:14, the team saw database connection timeouts. At 14:21, they rolled back the release, but the error rate did not recover. At 14:32, they discovered that the DNS resolver was returning a stale address for one of the primary database replicas. At 14:41, they failed over to the secondary replica and traffic recovered. At 14:59, error rate returned to baseline and the incident was closed.
segments.textReply: I’ll append the later investigation and recovery events alongside the existing timeline without inferring the release’s role.The timeline now shows that rollback did not restore service; failover followed the stale replica DNS discovery.

segments.text: The direct cause was a combination of two changes. The release reduced the connection pool timeout from five seconds to two seconds, which made the service less tolerant of slow DNS. Separately, a network change on Monday had reduced the DNS cache TTL, so the resolver was more likely to return stale records during a failover. The stale record pointed to a replica that had been taken out of service.
segments.textReply: I’m adding the two contributing changes and their interaction as a causal chain, while keeping them distinct from the timeline.

segments.text: The service kept retrying the stale address, and the shortened timeout turned a slowdown into a hard failure. Why did the rollback not fix it? Because the DNS record was already cached, and the rollback did not flush the resolver cache. The team assumed the release was the only change. The runbook said to roll back first, then check dependencies, but it did not say to verify DNS after a rollback.
segments.textReply: I’m adding the failure mechanism and the rollback/process gap as two linked explanations.The board now captures why rollback alone failed and the missing DNS verification step in the runbook.

segments.text: That is a process gap. The on call had the authority to fail over, but they waited for the database team because the runbook described failover as a last resort. That added about nine minutes. Detection was also slower than it should have been. The latency alert fired at 14:03, but it was a warning, not a page. The error rate alert paged at 14:07. We had no synthetic check for card payments from an external region.
segments.textReply: I’ve recorded the roughly nine-minute escalation delay and the warning-only latency alert, plus the missing external synthetic check.

If we had a synthetic payment probe, we might have caught the failure at 14:05. Customer impact. About eighteen thousand payment attempts failed. Most were retried successfully within ten minutes. Four hundred customers saw a duplicate authorization hold, which we reversed automatically by 16:30.

shapes.title: Post-session summary · Payment API outage
shapes.html:
Payment API outage · Tuesday postmortem
Purpose: understand the outage’s technical and process conditions, agree preventive actions, and review them to closure—blamelessly.
Core mechanism
Release shortened the connection-pool timeout from 5s to 2s; Monday’s reduced DNS cache TTL made stale records more likely. Cached DNS pointed to a retired replica; retries plus the shorter timeout turned slowdown into hard failure. Rollback did not flush resolver cache, so failover restored traffic.
Decision & severity
Sev-1: payment impact exceeded 30 minutes. Quarterly error budget is exhausted under agreed policy—not as punishment. Payment-path feature changes require reliability review before release. Preserve clear incident-channel structure and automatic duplicate-hold reversal.
Agreed action register
ActionOwnerDeadline
Synthetic payment probe from 2 regions, every minuteReliability team2 weeks
DNS health on payment dashboard; resolver-cache checks in runbookPlatform team1 week
Restore pool timeout to 5s; 30-minute canary before full rolloutPayments team3 days
Explicit on-call DB failover authority; update escalation policyEngineering manager1 week
Status-page template and communications rotationSupport2 weeks
Post-deploy DNS verification in release checklistRelease engineering2 weeks
RFC: resolver sidecar or DNS-independent service discovery (design only)Platform team6 weeks
Follow-up & process
Review actions weekly until closed. Two-week review checks the probe, runbook, canary and status-page template. At-risk owners notify the meeting lead before Friday. Process standards: 5-minute pre-deploy DNS/DB health check; canary timeout, pool and retry changes; distinct Sev-1 incident commander; first status-page update target 15 minutes.
Risks / open checks
Verify alerting reflects whole payment-path attempts, including those that never reach the service. Single resolver path remains an architectural risk; RFC is design only, implementation separate. Confirm ownership and dates for any process standards not covered by the assigned action register.
Compact timeline · UTC: 13:55 release → 14:03 latency warning → 14:07 >5% errors / outage starts → 14:21 rollback (no recovery) → 14:32 stale DNS found → 14:41 failover / traffic recovers → 14:59 baseline / incident closed. Status page updated 14:26.
